title: Sales follow-up automation that follows the buyer's next step
summary: Design follow-up automation around buyer commitments, fresh deal context and review controls. Includes a workflow specification and example.
body_markdown:
Sales follow-up automation should turn a buyer conversation into a relevant, timed next action. That requires more than generating an email: the system needs to understand the commitment, check what has changed, select the right channel and let the rep review the result.


A fixed sequence can be useful for a repeatable outreach motion. An active opportunity is different. A buyer who asked for a security document needs the document; a buyer who said “come back after our October planning meeting” needs the timing respected. Sending both people the same three-day reminder creates activity without necessarily advancing either deal.


## Start with a commitment record


After a meeting, capture what was agreed, who owns it, when it is due and the evidence. Separate explicit commitments from suggested actions.


Field Fictional example


Buyer commitment Finance will review the business case next Thursday


Seller commitment Send the implementation estimate before that review


Owner Account executive, with solutions engineer input


Due date Tuesday, in the buyer's time zone


Source Meeting transcript at the relevant timestamp


Missing information Finance reviewer has not been named


The missing reviewer is a question to resolve, not a blank to fill with a guessed contact. The automation can draft a request for an introduction while preparing the promised material.


## Define the trigger and the stop conditions together


“After every meeting, draft a follow-up” is a trigger. A usable workflow also explains which meetings qualify, where the draft goes and when the system should stop.


Specify the opportunity stage, meeting type and participants. An internal account review should not produce a customer email. A meeting that was canceled should not be summarized as though it happened.


Before creating a later follow-up, check for a new reply, another meeting, a completed task, a changed owner, a closed opportunity or an explicit request to pause. A follow-up that was sensible on Monday can be wrong by Wednesday. Keep the next action tied to the latest account activity, not just to the time since the last outbound message.


## Give each message a reason to exist


A useful follow-up connects three things: the buyer's stated problem, the action the seller promised and the decision the buyer needs to make.


Here is a fictional draft:


> Maya — you mentioned that your operations team spends Friday reconciling exceptions across three systems. I've attached the implementation outline we discussed, including how we would handle those exceptions during the pilot.
>
>
> Before finance reviews it next Thursday, could you introduce us to the person checking the implementation assumptions? We can address those questions in the same thread.


That message is specific without inventing ROI. It asks for one next step. It also gives the rep concrete facts to verify before sending: the pain, the attachment, the date and the intended recipient.


A prompt like “make it personalized” does not define those checks. A drafting rubric does.


## Review the work where the rep already works


Decide whether the output should be a Gmail draft, a task in a sales workspace or a message in an existing customer Slack channel. Use the channel where the relevant conversation is happening, subject to the team's permissions and preferences.


For each output, make the recipient, thread, attachments and proposed timing visible. Separate creating a draft from sending it. If a system can send automatically, that should be a deliberate workflow choice with clear limits—not an accidental consequence of approving the writing style.


When evaluating a tool, test whether the rep can correct the actual draft without copying the text between several apps. Also test what happens when the rep changes an instruction: is it applied to this message, this account or future messages? Those are different scopes.


## Measure execution quality before revenue impact


Start with a small set of observable measures:


- Time from a qualifying meeting to a reviewable draft.
- Percentage of promised actions completed by the agreed date.
- Percentage of drafts needing factual correction.
- Wrong-recipient, wrong-thread and duplicate-draft incidents.
- Useful buyer replies, using a defined classification.
- Rep review time per completed follow-up.


A faster draft is not automatically a faster buyer response. Report those metrics separately. A reply saying “please stop emailing me” should not count as the same success as a confirmed next meeting.


For revenue outcomes, compare similar opportunities over a sufficient observation period. Deal mix, rep experience and seasonality can change at the same time as the automation.


## A workflow specification to reuse


Write one paragraph covering: qualifying event; required context; promised action; output channel; review owner; stop conditions; escalation when information is missing; and success metric.


For example: “After an external discovery meeting on an open opportunity, prepare a follow-up from the transcript, current account activity and approved playbook. Include only supported commitments. Save it for the opportunity owner to review. Before any later reminder, recheck replies and stage. If the promised attachment is missing, create a task rather than claiming it is attached.”


Cedar connects deal context with drafting and agent workflows. A useful demo is to bring one real follow-up process and test the whole chain—from the buyer's commitment to the draft and the next scheduled action.

## Keep the review in the existing inbox


Cedar can prepare provider drafts in the connected mailbox, including Gmail. The rep can review the draft in the workflow they already use. Confirm the intended thread and recipient, and preserve edits the rep has made. A draft being created is not a message being sent; measure those events separately.
